newsitem.title: USA: House Democrats attack Republican tax bill.
newsitem.headline: House Democrats attack Republican tax bill.

text.p: House Democrats attacked Republican tax legislation Tuesday, but were unable to agree on their own plan to offer as an alternative.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer Monday proposed a plan to cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years as part of the overall budget pact reached by congressional leaders and President Clinton last month.
The Texas Republican's legislation was expected to be considered by the House Ways and Means Committee Wednesday, where amendments will be offered.
But Democrats, including President Clinton, were quick to attack the tax bill, saying it favoured corporations and the wealthy over lower-income families.
Archer said his bill would provide the most benefit to the middle class, with $53.8 billion of the tax relief going to people with annual incomes between $40,000 and $75,000.
House Democrats met late in the day and after being presented with three alternatives members were divided.
House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri said he still expected a Democratic tax bill would be offered in the House Ways and Means Committee.
"One of the outrages here is that we're having to do this so quickly, I mean it would be nice if we had a little more time," Gephardt said.

Representative Charles Rangel of New York, the ranking Democrat on the House tax-writing panel, has proposed a tax cut plan that would allocate half of the package to education tax initiatives and a child tax credit.

Representative Collin Peterson, a Democrat from Minnesota and co-chair of the "Blue Dogs," a group of conservative Democrats, said their proposal would end up with about $50 billion left over of a $250 billion net tax cut over 10 years that was part of the budget agreement. The leftover amount would go toward further deficit reduction, he said.

The third Democratic proposal, offered by Representative Jim McDermott of Washington, would return to workers 2 percent of the first $20,000 in wages, so in essence anyone with that income or higher would get $400 back a year.
While realistically a Democratic tax plan has little chance of full implementation in a Republican-controlled Congress, the drafting of legislation showed the level of discontent.
A provision of Archer's plan that was expected to run into opposition even from Republicans would scale back the ethanol tax subsidy, analysts said.
House Majority Leader Dick Armey, a Texas Republican, said Archer's plan was a starting point.

"This is the chairman's mark, the basis by which they proceed in committee," Armey said. "I think Bill has done an outstanding job. He has taken a world of expectations and made them fit into very tough constraints," he added.
Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, was writing his own version of a five-year tax cut plan that will differ from Archer's proposal.

Robert Reischauer, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, said the real wrangling will occur when the House and Senate tax bills are in "conference," where differences between the two are worked out.
"The real battle will not occur until conference because at that point the president's lieutenants will come in and say 'if that stays in it we'll veto the bill'," Reischauer said.
Republicans are likely to stick by their capital gains provisions but may give in on education tax initiatives if necessary to avoid a presidential veto, Reischauer predicted.
